title: AGENTS.md - Project Guide
content: # AGENTS.md - Project Guide## Project OverviewPersonal portfolio website for **Shanmuga Sundaram Natarajan (Shan)** — a Hands-on Architect & Technical Leader with 19+ years of experience. The site is built with Jekyll and hosted on GitHub Pages at `shanmugasundaram.in`.## Tech Stack- **Static Site Generator**: Jekyll (via `github-pages` gem ~228)- **Hosting**: GitHub Pages (branch: `gh-pages`)- **Styling**: Custom CSS (no Sass preprocessing beyond Jekyll's front matter wrapper in `style.scss`)- **Icons**: Font Awesome 6.4.0 (CDN)- **Fonts**: Google Fonts — Inter, Space Grotesk, Open Sans, Raleway- **Ruby version**: see `.ruby-version`## Project Structure```_config.yml # Jekyll config (site title, author, plugins, social links)_layouts/ default.html # Base layout: header, nav, footer, theme-switcher script home.html # Homepage: hero, about preview, skills grid, featured projects, blog posts page.html # Generic page layout with hero banner post.html # Blog post layout_data/ projects.yml # Project data (title, description, image, technologies, links)_posts/ # Blog posts (Markdown)_plugins/ reading_time.rb # Custom Liquid filter for estimated reading timeassets/ css/ style.scss # Main stylesheet (~985 lines) — CSS variables, components, responsive theme-switcher.css # Theme & mode toggle styles, theme color/font variables js/ theme-switcher.js # Dark/light mode toggle images/ # Project screenshots, profile photo, logoindex.md # Homepage (uses home layout)about.md # About page with professional experience, skills, educationprojects.md # Projects page (iterates _data/projects.yml)contact.md # Contact pageblog/index.md # Blog listing404.md # Custom 404 pageCNAME # Custom domain: shanmugasundaram.inserve.py # Python dev server for static preview (serves _site/)```## Key Architecture Decisions- **No default theme** (`theme: null` in `_config.yml`) — all styling is custom CSS- **CSS variables** for theming — colors, spacing, typography defined in `:root`- **Single color theme**: `orange-red`, set via a fixed `data-theme="orange-red"` attribute on `` (no theme picker UI)- **Dark/light mode**: toggled via `data-mode` attribute on ``, persisted in localStorage- **Fixed header** with scroll effect and mobile hamburger menu- **Glass-morphism cards** (`card-glass`) with backdrop-filter blur## Development Workflow1. **Recommended**: Edit locally, push to GitHub, GitHub Actions builds and deploys automatically2. **Docker**: `docker run --rm -it --volume="$PWD:/srv/jekyll" --publish 4000:4000 jekyll/jekyll jekyll serve`3. **Python server**: `bundle exec jekyll build && python3 serve.py` (static preview only on port 4000)**Note**: `eventmachine` gem has compilation issues on macOS/Apple Silicon, so local `jekyll serve` may not work.## Common Tasks- **Add a project**: Edit `_data/projects.yml`, add image to `assets/images/projects/`- **Add a blog post**: Create `_posts/YYYY-MM-DD-title.md` with front matter- **Modify navigation**: Edit `_layouts/default.html` (nav-links section)- **Change theme colors**: Edit `assets/css/theme-switcher.css` (`[data-theme="..."]` blocks)- **Change base styles**: Edit `assets/css/style.scss`## Style Conventions- CSS uses BEM-like naming (`.project-card`, `.project-title`, `.project-content`)- CSS variables follow `--color-*`, `--space-*`, `--font-size-*`, `--radius-*` naming- Layouts use Liquid templating with Jekyll variables (`{% raw %}{{ site.* }}{% endraw %}`, `{% raw %}{{ page.* }}{% endraw %}`)- Content pages use Markdown with YAML front matter (`layout`, `title`, `description`, `permalink`)- HTML in content pages uses utility classes: `grid grid-2`, `card card-glass`, `text-center`, `mt-xl`

title: The Runner Has No LLM: A Deterministic Pipeline for Claude Code
description: A dependency-free Node runner drives ten Claude Code agents through fresh sessions, a spec-to-test trace and four human gates. How it works, where it breaks.
excerpt: Ten AI agents write the research, specs, design, tests and code for one change in my delivery pipeline, and none of them decides what happens next. A plain Node program does. It reads a status command, starts the next agent, runs checks that involve no model, and stops at four points where a huma...
content: Ten AI agents write the research, specs, design, tests and code for one change in my delivery pipeline, and none of them decides what happens next. A plain Node program does. It reads a status command, starts the next agent, runs checks that involve no model, and stops at four points where a human has to say yes. The model still produces the inputs to those decisions, and I mark where that matters.This post opens that program up. It is about 2,150 lines of JavaScript with no npm dependencies, and it is open source. I wrote about what happened when I ran it in a separate post, including a stuck loop and an override I regret. Here I stay with the code and the design reasons, because they are the part you can reuse.How to read this. If agents and specs are new to you, start at the next section and read through “One idea, start to finish”. If you write code, jump to “A session is a function call”. If you design systems, the sections on gates, the trace check and “Where this does not fit” carry the trade-offs. Terms are defined where they first appear.The runner decides, the agents writeThe reliable parts of a multi-agent pipeline are the parts where the model gets no vote. In this kit, an agent never chooses the next step and never directly approves a gate. The model writes files, and code decides what happens around those files. The model does still supply some inputs to those decisions: it ticks its own task checkboxes, it proposes the risk tier, and it writes the review that can block a merge. Those are the weak points, and a later section lists them.That split gives four properties: Control flow is ordinary code. The loop that moves a change through stages is a while loop in bin/agentic.mjs. You can read it, test it and step through it in a debugger. A document is “done” when the file exists and validates. The runner asks the OpenSpec CLI whether an artifact is finished. It does not take the agent’s word for it. Checks are deterministic. Validation, task completion, the project’s test command and a spec-to-test trace all run as code. Humans approve at fixed points. Four gates, with a policy that depends on a risk level.Each agent is a fresh headless session: a new claude -p process with an empty context that runs one job and exits. Agents never talk to each other. They read and write one shared folder. If you are a beginner, think of it as a relay race where the baton is a directory of Markdown files and the referee is a script.OpenSpec in five minutesOpenSpec is a spec-driven development framework: you and the AI agree on what to build, in writing, before any code is written. It is MIT-licensed, installs from npm as @fission-ai/openspec (Node 20.19 or later) and, per its README, works with 30-plus AI coding assistants through slash commands. I used version 1.15.0 in October 2026.It adds a plain-Markdown layer to a repository, with four ideas: Concept What it is Spec A Markdown file of requirements, each with scenarios written as WHEN/THEN. Specs live in openspec/specs/ and describe what the system does today. Change One folder per feature or fix under openspec/changes/<id>/. Proposed work stays separate from the current truth. Delta spec Inside a change, a spec file that lists only what is ADDED, MODIFIED, REMOVED or RENAMED, instead of rewriting a whole spec. Archive When a change is done, it moves to openspec/changes/archive/ and its deltas merge into the main specs, so the specs keep up with the code. A change holds proposal.md (why and what), specs/ (the deltas), design.md (how) and tasks.md (a checklist). Here is a small delta spec, in the format the CLI validates:## ADDED Requirements### Requirement: PAY-012 Refund windowThe system SHALL allow a partner to refund a settled payout within 30 days of settlement.#### Scenario: Refund inside the window- **WHEN** a partner requests a refund 10 days after settlement- **THEN** the refund is created and the payout balance is reduced#### Scenario: Refund outside the window- **WHEN** a partner requests a refund 31 days after settlement- **THEN** the request is rejected with the error code REFUND_WINDOW_CLOSEDThe core flow uses /opsx:explore, /opsx:propose, /opsx:apply and /opsx:archive, and an expanded profile adds /opsx:verify, /opsx:ff and others. The README compares itself with GitHub Spec Kit (more phases, more setup) and Kiro (tied to one IDE). That is the project’s own positioning, so weigh it as such.What OpenSpec does not give you is an orchestrator. It has no loop that runs the next step, no cost cap, no approval gates and no tests that tie requirements to code. That gap is what the kit fills, and it does so with three pieces of OpenSpec’s own machinery: A custom schema. OpenSpec lets you define the artifact list. The kit’s agentic-sdlc schema adds research, threat-model, test-plan, verification and retrospective around the default four. openspec status as the scheduler. title: Loop Engineering Is Not the Agent Loop: Data From Two Runs
description: Loop engineering now means the system above your agents, not the tool loop inside one. Cost and failure data from two runs of my OpenSpec pipeline.
excerpt: In one change on my agentic delivery pipeline, at least six consecutive implementer sessions reported the same three tasks as still open. Every guard I had configured worked: the retry counters capped the passes, the budget cap held, and the run ended. Yet nothing in the system noticed it was goi...
content: In one change on my agentic delivery pipeline, at least six consecutive implementer sessions reported the same three tasks as still open. Every guard I had configured worked: the retry counters capped the passes, the budget cap held, and the run ended. Yet nothing in the system noticed it was going in circles, and a human revision restarted the same cycle.That run changed how I use the word loop. In my August post I used it for the turn-by-turn cycle inside one agent: call the model, run a tool, feed the result back. That meaning is still valid. But the industry has since taken the same word for something one level up, and my pipeline lives almost entirely in that upper level. Below I correct my own terminology, then use two real runs, with their costs and failures, to show what the upper level looks like when it breaks.I’ll say up front what this is. The evidence is two changes on one small todo app, run on my laptop through a pipeline I wrote. It is a small sample from one system, not a benchmark. The mechanisms are what generalize, so those are what I’ll focus on.Two things people call a loopLoop engineering, in the 2026 sense, is the system that decides what an agent works on next, checks the result and decides what happens after that. Addy Osmani named and defined it in an essay on 7 June 2026. His description is a system that finds work, assigns it, checks it, records progress and decides what comes next, so that the system prompts the agents and you don’t. He places it relative to the harness in one line: loop engineering “sits one floor above the harness.”What I wrote about in August is the inner loop. The model is called, it asks for a tool, the harness checks permission, the tool runs, the result goes back, and the cycle repeats until the model stops or a cap is hit. Call that the agent loop. It runs inside a single session.The two operate at different scales and fail differently:   Agent loop (inner) Loop engineering (outer) Unit of work One model turn One task, change or ticket Lives in A single session The system that starts and ends sessions Decides Which tool to call next What to work on, when to retry, who verifies, when to stop, when to ask a human Typical stop condition end_turn, iteration cap Verified result, retry budget, cost cap, human gate Typical failure Runaway tool calls Retrying what cannot succeed, accepting “done” without proof Other write-ups describe the same split. codecentric stacks three layers: context engineering at the bottom, harness engineering in the middle, loop engineering on top. Future AGI gives a diagnostic I’ll use later: if a bad run “tried the right thing and could not execute it cleanly,” suspect the harness, and if it “kept repeating itself,” suspect the loop. The kit is a Node runner with no dependencies (bin/agentic.mjs). It takes a one-line idea and drives it through research, proposal, specs, design, threat model, test plan, tasks, build, verification, code review and a retrospective. title: Stop Using a Language Model for Everything. Here's What I Use Instead.
description: Most enterprise agent pipelines route every AI call through an LLM. After profiling a production pipeline, I found 80% of those calls were structured decision work that didn't need generative capability at all. Here's what I use instead, and when.
excerpt: Most enterprise agent pipelines start from the same assumption: the AI layer is an LLM, every call goes through it, and the only open question is which one. I built a production pipeline on that assumption, and after running it for a while I started to doubt it.
content: Most enterprise agent pipelines start from the same assumption: the AI layer is an LLM, every call goes through it, and the only open question is which one. I built a production pipeline on that assumption, and after running it for a while I started to doubt it.I profiled the calls and about 80% of the AI work was structured decision-making: classify this intent, score this document for relevance, pull these fields out of some messy input. No human ever read those outputs. They went straight into the next system. So I was paying frontier prices and waiting on LLM latency for work that didn’t need generation at all. Every so often the model also invented a field that wasn’t in the input, which is what you get when nothing in the architecture stops it.That made me look at Jev, released in September 2026 by TypeSafe AI, founded by Diogo Almeida (formerly OpenAI).What System One Models Actually AreLLMs are trained with RLHF. The optimization target is outputs human raters prefer, which makes them excellent at generation and structurally overconfident. Uncertain answers score poorly with human raters even when uncertainty is the accurate state. The output is always a string. Your code parses it, validates it, and lives with the fact that there’s always a path where the model produces well-formatted nonsense.Jev uses RLCD, Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions. You define the output schema in advance. The model selects from that space and returns a typed value with a calibrated confidence score. There’s no generative step. The model cannot produce an output that violates the schema because the schema is the entire output space. TypeSafe describes it as “a frontier-intelligence function call: unstructured state in, typed probabilistic decisions out.”The calibration is as important as the typing. An LLM prompted to express confidence tends to express consistent confidence, not accurate confidence. Calibrated means when Jev reports 90% confidence, it’s right 90% of the time statistically across those calls. That becomes a real architectural control surface: you set the threshold for autonomous action versus escalation, and the threshold is meaningful.What This Looks Like in CodeReal agent pipelines run two kinds of work through the same model: decisions at the edges and synthesis at the core. Jev takes the decisions, and an LLM stays on anything a person will read. The confidence threshold ties the two together. With an LLM, “escalate if unsure” means prompt engineering and hoping the model reports its own uncertainty honestly. With Jev, it’s a numeric cutoff on a calibrated score, so you can set it and test it.flowchart TD A([Incoming Query]) --> B["Jev: Intent Classification<br/>70–500ms · $0.042/MTok"] B --> C{Confidence<br/>Score} C -->|"> 0.85 · High confidence"| D["Route Directly<br/>Structured action"] C -->|"< 0.85 · Low confidence"| E["Escalate to LLM<br/>Claude / GPT"] E --> F["Synthesis + Generation<br/>Output a human reads"] D --> G([Pipeline continues]) F --> GHere’s a routing step from a RAG intake pipeline. The before version uses an LLM to classify whether an incoming query needs retrieval:# Before: LLM call, parse string, hope it says yes or noresponse = claude.messages.create( model="claude-sonnet-5-5", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Does this query need retrieval? {query}"}])needs_retrieval = "yes" in response.content[0].text.lower()The failure here is easy to miss because the output looks fine. The model might say “Yes, retrieval is needed” or “Retrieval would be appropriate here” or add caveats that break the parse. The Jev version:# After: Jev typed decision with calibrated confidenceresult = jev.decide( input=query, schema={ "needs_retrieval": {"type": "bool"}, "category": {"type": "enum", "values": ["billing", "technical", "general"]} })if result.confidence > 0.85: route_autonomously(result.needs_retrieval, result.category)else: escalate_to_llm(query)It’s cleaner, but that’s the smaller benefit. A bad schema fails when you define it instead of quietly misbehaving in production, and the confidence check is a real number, not a string you hoped to parse.The Cost and Latency GapFrontier LLMs run $0.20 to $10 per million input tokens with response times of 3 to 329 seconds. Jev is $0.042 per million tokens, responds in 70 to 500ms, and output tokens are free.For classification, routing, and structured extraction workloads, that’s roughly 100x cheaper and 40 to 200x faster. TypeSafe published results from Jack and Jill, a hiring platform: they replaced an LLM-based candidate screening pipeline with Jev and got 88% cost reduction, 2x throughput, and 10 days from test to production.Workflows Where Jev Changes the MathEach workflow below follows the same layout: what it does, the flow, then the code. title: Harness Engineering and Loop Engineering: The Layer Between an LLM and Real Work
description: Prompt engineering gets a language model to say the right thing once. Harness engineering and loop engineering get it to do the right thing repeatedly, safely, and to completion, explained from first principles, with a worked example, using Claude Code's observable behavior as the reference.
excerpt: First, what is an AI agent? The term gets thrown around loosely. It’s a language model (an LLM, the kind of AI behind ChatGPT or Claude) that does more than answer a question once. It can take actions such as reading a file, running a command or searching the web, look at what happened, and decid...
content:
First, what is an AI agent? The term gets thrown around loosely. It’s a language model (an LLM, the kind of AI behind ChatGPT or Claude) that does more than answer a question once. It can take actions such as reading a file, running a command or searching the web, look at what happened, and decide what to do next, in a loop, until the task is done. A chatbot takes one input and gives one output. An agent can keep acting, unsupervised, for as long as it takes.That’s what makes agents useful, and also what makes them risky. Prompt engineering is about wording your instructions so a model gives a good answer in a single response. That’s necessary, but it isn’t enough once the model is acting on its own, reading its own results, deciding what to do next and deciding when to stop. At that point a second discipline appears. The question changes from “what do I say to the model?” to “what do I build around it?”I call the two halves harness engineering and loop engineering. People often lump both together as “the agent,” but they’re different things. The harness is everything the model is allowed to do, which tools it can call, what files it can touch, what commands are off-limits, how much context it sees before it even starts. The loop is the control flow that keeps calling the model, checking what it wants to do, letting it (or not), feeding the result back, and deciding when to stop.Get the harness wrong and a capable model can do dangerous or useless things simply because nobody told it not to. Get the loop wrong and a well-behaved model can still run forever, burn through your budget, or drift off the original task because nothing was watching for it.This post explains both from first principles, then walks through one example: an agent that auto-fixes failing tests in a pull request. I’ll use Claude Code (permission modes, hooks, subagents, on-demand tool loading and CLAUDE.md instructions) as the running reference, since I use it every day.A few termsIf you’ve built with LLM APIs before, skip this. If not, these five terms come up a lot: Context window, the total amount of text (measured in tokens, roughly word-fragments) a model can “see” at once, including its instructions, the conversation so far, and anything it just read. It’s finite, usually a few hundred thousand tokens, and everything you put in it costs money and pushes out room for something else. System prompt, a block of instructions given to the model before the conversation starts, setting its role, rules, and boundaries. The user never sees it directly; it shapes how the model behaves throughout. Tool call / tool use, when a model, instead of just replying with text, asks to run a specific action, “call the Bash tool with this command”, and waits for the result before continuing. This is the mechanism that turns a chatbot into an agent. MCP (Model Context Protocol), a standard way to plug external systems (Slack, a database, Google Drive) into an agent as tools, without writing custom integration code for each one. Sandbox, a restricted environment (limited filesystem access, no network, a disposable container) that limits what a tool call can actually affect, even if the model asks for something dangerous.Two failure modesThe easiest way to see why they’re separate is to look at what breaks when you skip each one.Skip the harness and the model has no boundaries. It can call any tool with any argument, read files outside the project, run destructive shell commands or leak sensitive output. It isn’t malicious. Nothing told it not to. I call this a scope failure: it did something it should never have been allowed to try.Skip the loop design and the model has boundaries but no brakes. It re-reads the same file five times, retries a failing action endlessly, or keeps going “one more turn” until the conversation has been summarised so many times that it forgets what it was asked to do. I call this a termination failure: each action was allowed, but nothing made it stop.%%{init: {'theme': 'dark', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#313244', 'primaryTextColor': '#CDD6F4', 'primaryBorderColor': '#89B4FA', 'lineColor': '#A6ADC8', 'secondaryColor': '#1E1E2E', 'background': '#1E1E2E', 'mainBkg': '#313244', 'clusterBkg': '#24243E', 'clusterBorder': '#45475A', 'titleColor': '#CDD6F4', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#1E1E2E', 'fontFamily': 'JetBrains Mono, monospace', 'fontSize': '13px'}}}%%flowchart LR classDef harness fill:#1A2A3A,stroke:#89B4FA,color:#89B4FA classDef loop fill:#2A1A3A,stroke:#CBA6F7,color:#CBA6F7 classDef model fill:#313244,stroke:#A6ADC8,color:#CDD6F4 subgraph H["Harness — what the model is allowed to touch"] T["Tool registry

description: A deep technical walkthrough of SDLC Factory, an autonomous AI pipeline that transforms plain-English product ideas into production-ready software through 10 specialized agents, structured artifact contracts, and human-in-the-loop governance gates.
excerpt: Software delivery loses information at every handoff. content:
Software delivery loses information at every handoff. An idea starts out clear in someone’s head, goes through six meetings, three Confluence pages and a Jira backlog nobody reads, and ends up as code that solves last quarter’s version of the problem. Even good teams lose time and detail at each boundary between product, architecture, development and QA.Over the last few months I’ve been building something to attack this: SDLC Factory. It takes a plain-English product idea and drives it through a full delivery pipeline using 10 specialised AI agents, enforced artifact contracts between stages, and human approval gates at the points that matter.It’s more than a chatbot wrapper. It has parallel development threads, a QA auto-fix loop, context compression for long conversations, prompt injection scanning, multi-tenant isolation and a cost tracker. This post covers how I built it, the design decisions that mattered, and what I got wrong the first time.What’s wrong with the usual approachesMost AI coding agents I’ve seen fall into one of two camps: Single-agent loops. One model does everything: requirements, design, code and tests. It forgets what it decided three pages ago and writes code that doesn’t match its own spec. Unstructured multi-agent systems. Agents spawn sub-agents freely and coordinate in natural language. It sounds powerful, but in my experience the coordination overhead eats the gains and debugging is painful.Neither guarantees that the output of one stage is valid input for the next. Requirements drift from the architecture, and the architecture drifts from the code. There’s no contract.SDLC Factory enforces one. Every stage produces a JSON artifact validated against a schema, and the next stage gets only what it needs from earlier stages. It never sees the raw conversation history.System architectureHere’s how the whole system fits together:%%{init: {'theme': 'dark', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#313244', 'primaryTextColor': '#CDD6F4', 'primaryBorderColor': '#89B4FA', 'lineColor': '#A6ADC8', 'secondaryColor': '#1E1E2E', 'background': '#1E1E2E', 'mainBkg': '#313244', 'clusterBkg': '#24243E', 'clusterBorder': '#45475A', 'titleColor': '#CDD6F4', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#1E1E2E', 'fontFamily': 'JetBrains Mono, monospace', 'fontSize': '13px'}}}%%flowchart TB classDef entry fill:#1A3A2A,stroke:#A6E3A1,color:#A6E3A1 classDef orch fill:#1A2A3A,stroke:#89B4FA,color:#89B4FA classDef agent fill:#2A1A3A,stroke:#CBA6F7,color:#CBA6F7 classDef tool fill:#3A2A1A,stroke:#FAB387,color:#FAB387 classDef mem fill:#3A1A2A,stroke:#F38BA8,color:#F38BA8 classDef db fill:#2A3A1A,stroke:#A6E3A1,color:#A6E3A1 classDef gw fill:#1A3A3A,stroke:#94E2D5,color:#94E2D5 classDef tel fill:#3A3A1A,stroke:#F9E2AF,color:#F9E2AF subgraph Entry["Entry Points"] CLI["CLI · sdlc.py"]:::entry API["Web API · FastAPI"]:::entry WH["Webhook · HITL callback"]:::entry QUE["Programmatic · ApprovalQueue"]:::entry end subgraph Orch["Pipeline Orchestrator core/pipeline.py"] SM["Stage machine · artifact routing

title: Why Most Teams Fail at Collaboration, And How Domain-Driven Design Fixes It
description: Three teams. One database column. Three different mental models, until it all broke at 2am. Here's how Domain-Driven Design gives you the structures that make collaboration actually work at scale.
excerpt: Here’s a bug that took three weeks to track down.
content: Here’s a bug that took three weeks to track down.The backend team added a status column to the users table to track onboarding progress, steps 0 to 4. The frontend team read the same field as a boolean: account active or not. The data team exported it weekly and sorted users into cold, warm and hot engagement tiers.Nobody documented any of this, because nobody thought they needed to. The column was called status, after all.Then a badly timed migration broke the frontend and corrupted the analytics pipeline, and the on-call engineer spent three weeks digging through git history to work out why.Collaboration failures are like that. They hide in the gap between what you think a word means and what your colleague thinks it means, and you usually find them during a production incident at 2am.%%{init: {'theme': 'dark', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#313244', 'primaryTextColor': '#CDD6F4', 'primaryBorderColor': '#45475A', 'lineColor': '#A6ADC8', 'background': '#1E1E2E', 'mainBkg': '#313244', 'clusterBkg': '#24243E', 'fontFamily': 'JetBrains Mono, monospace', 'fontSize': '13px'}}}%%graph TD classDef yellow fill:#313244,stroke:#F9E2AF,color:#F9E2AF classDef blue fill:#313244,stroke:#89B4FA,color:#89B4FA classDef green fill:#1A3A1A,stroke:#A6E3A1,color:#A6E3A1 classDef red fill:#2E1A1A,stroke:#F38BA8,color:#F38BA8 classDef mauve fill:#313244,stroke:#CBA6F7,color:#CBA6F7 classDef teal fill:#313244,stroke:#94E2D5,color:#94E2D5 classDef dim fill:#1E1E2E,stroke:#45475A,color:#A6ADC8 FIELD["users.status<br/>one column,<br/>zero documentation"]:::yellow FIELD --> BE["Backend<br/>status = onboarding step<br/>0 · 1 · 2 · 3 · 4"]:::blue FIELD --> FE["Frontend<br/>status = account live?<br/>true · false"]:::blue FIELD --> DA["Analytics<br/>status = engagement tier<br/>cold · warm · hot"]:::blue BE --> OOF["💥 3-week incident<br/>Nobody was lying.<br/>Nobody was wrong.<br/>Nobody talked."]:::red FE --> OOF DA --> OOF OOF --> LESSON["The problem wasn't technical.<br/>It was a missing shared model."]:::dimIt’s not a people problem. It’s a structure problem.Most managers read this as a communication failure and reach for process: more standups, mandatory documentation, a new Confluence page that everyone writes once and nobody reads again.I’ve seen this at startups, mid-sized companies and big enterprises. Agile ceremonies don’t fix it. Retrospectives surface it but don’t solve it. That’s because it isn’t really a people or process problem. It’s a structural one.When teams don’t share a model of the domain they work in, every handoff is a translation, and nobody realises they’re translating. People assume they speak the same language because they use the same words. They don’t.This is what Domain-Driven Design (DDD) addresses. Eric Evans introduced the term in 2003 and the core idea is deceptively simple: the structure of your software should reflect the structure of the business. Not the structure of your database. Not the structure of your org chart from three reorgs ago. The actual domain, the problem space your business exists to solve.What I find most useful about DDD is how seriously it takes language.Shared language is an architecture decisionDDD calls this Ubiquitous Language. Engineers, product managers, designers and analysts all use the same vocabulary for the domain. title: Building RAG That Actually Works: Lessons from the Trenches
description: A practitioner's guide to building production-grade RAG pipelines, covering chunking strategy, retrieval tuning, re-ranking, and evaluation. Lessons from real failures, not sanitized tutorials.
excerpt: I’ve read probably a dozen RAG tutorials. They all do the same thing: show you how to embed a handful of PDFs into a vector store, run a similarity search, stuff the results into a prompt, and call it a production pipeline. content: I’ve read probably a dozen RAG tutorials. They all do the same thing: show you how to embed a handful of PDFs into a vector store, run a similarity search, stuff the results into a prompt, and call it a production pipeline. Then you try to use the same approach on real data, thousands of documents, mixed formats, users with messy natural language queries, and the whole thing falls apart. The answers are vague, wrong, or confidently referencing documents that have nothing to do with the question.That gap between “works in the tutorial” and “works in production” is what this post is about. I’ve built a few of these pipelines now, and I’ve made almost every mistake there is to make, wrong chunk sizes, no overlap, skipping the re-ranker, shipping without any evaluation. I’m going to walk through the full pipeline, from chunking to evaluation, not as a sanitized tutorial, but as the thing I wish I’d had when I started building this stuff for real.We’ll use LangChain, ChromaDB, and OpenAI throughout. If you use different tools, the concepts all transfer.The Two Phases You Need to Separate in Your HeadBefore any code, the most important mental model is that RAG is two completely separate systems that happen to share a vector database.The indexing pipeline is offline. It runs on a schedule or when documents change. It loads your source files, chunks them, converts them to embeddings, and writes them to a vector store. Speed isn’t critical here. Correctness is.The query pipeline is online. It runs on every user request, and it needs to be fast. It embeds the user’s question, retrieves the most relevant chunks, builds a prompt, and calls the LLM.%%{init: {'theme': 'dark', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#313244', 'primaryTextColor': '#CDD6F4', 'primaryBorderColor': '#89B4FA', 'lineColor': '#A6ADC8', 'secondaryColor': '#24243E', 'background': '#1E1E2E', 'mainBkg': '#313244', 'clusterBkg': '#24243E', 'clusterBorder': '#45475A', 'titleColor': '#CDD6F4', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#1E1E2E', 'fontFamily': 'JetBrains Mono, monospace', 'fontSize': '13px'}}}%%flowchart LR classDef yellow fill:#313244,stroke:#F9E2AF,color:#F9E2AF,rx:4 classDef blue fill:#313244,stroke:#89B4FA,color:#89B4FA,rx:4 classDef mauve fill:#313244,stroke:#CBA6F7,color:#CBA6F7,rx:4 classDef green fill:#1A3A1A,stroke:#A6E3A1,color:#A6E3A1,rx:4 classDef red fill:#313244,stroke:#F38BA8,color:#F38BA8,rx:4 subgraph OFFLINE["① OFFLINE · INDEXING"] A["Documents<br/>PDF / HTML / TXT"]:::yellow B["Document Loader"]:::blue C["Text Splitter<br/>chunk_size=1000, overlap=200"]:::blue D["Embedding Model<br/>text-embedding-3-large"]:::mauve A --> B --> C --> D end VS[("Vector Store<br/>ChromaDB")]:::green D --> VS subgraph ONLINE["② ONLINE · QUERY"] F["User Question"]:::yellow G["Embed Question"]:::blue H["Similarity Search<br/>MMR k=5, fetch_k=20"]:::blue I["Re-ranker<br/>cross-encoder top-5"]:::red J["Prompt Builder → LLM<br/>temperature=0"]:::green K(["Answer"]):::green F --> G --> H --> I --> J --> K end VS -->|top-k chunks| HKeeping these two phases decoupled is the first thing most tutorials get wrong. If your indexing and querying code are tangled together, you’ll end up in situations where you can’t re-index without restarting your query service, or where a slow re-embed job blocks user requests. Treat them as separate processes from day one.Here’s how to get your environment set up:# requirements.txt equivalent — install these first# pip install langchain langchain-openai langchain-chroma chromadb openai tiktoken pypdfimport osfrom pathlib import Path# Set your API keyos.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"] = "your-openai-api-key"# Verify environmentimport openaiimport chromadbimport langchainprint(f"LangChain version: {langchain.__version__}")print(f"ChromaDB version: {chromadb.__version__}")print("Environment ready")Run this and confirm your package versions before going further. It took me two weeks of debugging poor retrieval quality before I realized my chunks were the problem, not my embedding model or retrieval code. I had set chunk_size=2000 thinking “more context = better” and ended up with bloated, unfocused chunks that pulled in too much noise along with the relevant content.The intuition is simple. A chunk is the atomic unit of retrieval. When a user asks a question, the system fetches the N most relevant chunks and hands them to the LLM. title: Zero Vibe Coding with Claude Code Agents
description: How I built a production-ready Personal Finance Tracker entirely from the terminal using Claude Code CLI with a 9-agent, 5-track spec-driven pipeline, no UI MCP tools, no vibe coding.
excerpt: Most talk about AI-assisted coding ends up at “vibe coding”: throw a vague prompt at an LLM, plug in a UI tool, and hope the architecture holds together.
content: Most talk about AI-assisted coding ends up at “vibe coding”: throw a vague prompt at an LLM, plug in a UI tool, and hope the architecture holds together.I wanted to try the opposite. What happens if you treat the AI like a small engineering team with defined roles and rules? To find out, I built a Personal Finance Tracker entirely from the terminal, with no UI Model Context Protocol (MCP) integrations like Figma. I set up Claude Code CLI with nine agents, five pipeline tracks, parallel execution at four points, and five hooks that enforce quality rules at the filesystem level.You can check out the final codebase here: Personal Finance Tracker on GitHubThe Final ProductHere’s the finished app running locally, with a sidebar and separate pages for Dashboard, Transactions and Budgets. None of it came from a visual design tool:1. The Claude Code features I leaned onClaude Code works on your local filesystem, which gives you a few things a chat window can’t. These are the ones I used most: Custom Prompt Hooks (.claude/hooks/): A React app needs consistent linting, and AI output often gets the formatting slightly wrong. So I created a .claude/hooks/post-edit-lint.sh script. Every time Claude Code edited a .tsx or .ts file, the CLI automatically fired off $ESLINT_BIN --fix. After that, I stopped seeing CI builds fail on style errors. Persistent CLI Memory (.claude/agent-memory/): I stored detailed markdown files like DOMAIN-OWNERSHIP.md and hexagonal-architecture.md. Claude Code pulled this context in whenever I prompted it, so the code it wrote followed my architecture decisions. Context Compaction (/compact): A complex backend fills up the context quickly. Once Claude had finished planning a feature, I ran /compact, which shrinks the context but keeps the key points. That saved tokens and kept things quick. Intelligent Commits (/commit): After ./gradlew test passed, I ran /commit instead of writing the message myself. Claude Code read the actual git diff and wrote a sensible commit message. A simulated terminal run$ claude╭────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮│ Claude Code (v0.x.x) - Project: personal-finance-tracker │╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯▶ I want to add double-entry transfers between accounts. title: LLM Tokenizers: The Hidden Engine Behind AI Language Models
description: Tokenizers are the invisible foundation of every large language model, shaping context limits, API costs, cross-lingual fairness, and model reasoning. Here's how they work and why they matter.
content: A language model never sees your text. Before any neural network runs, the text is converted into numbers by a tokenizer. It’s easy to ignore, but it explains a lot about how LLMs behave and what they cost.What tokenization isThe tokenizer splits text into pieces called tokens and maps each one to an ID from a fixed vocabulary. “Hello, world!” might become [15496, 11, 995, 0]. Those four numbers are all the model gets.Why you should care Context windows are measured in tokens, not words or characters. API pricing is per token, so how efficiently your text tokenizes affects the bill. Some languages are penalised. Text in languages that tokenize poorly uses up more of the context window and costs more. Code, maths and prose all tokenize differently, which affects how much of each you can fit.Three approachesWord-basedSplit on spaces and punctuation. It’s intuitive and simple, but the vocabulary gets enormous, and any word the tokenizer hasn’t seen is a problem. Languages with lots of compound words, such as German, Finnish and Turkish, suffer the most.Character-basedEvery character is a token, so “Hello world” becomes 11 tokens. The vocabulary is tiny and nothing is ever unknown. But sequences get five to ten times longer than with words, and the model has to work out meaning from individual letters, which is expensive.SubwordThis is what modern models use, including GPT, Claude, Llama and Gemini. Words are broken into meaningful chunks: “Unlikeliest” might become ["Un", "likely", "est"].The most common algorithm is Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE): Start with single characters. Count how often each adjacent pair occurs. Merge the most frequent pair into a new token. Repeat until you reach the target vocabulary size, typically 10,000 to 100,000.Common words end up as single tokens, rare words get split into pieces you can recognise, and the vocabulary stays manageable.How it affects modelsCost. Training, fine-tuning and inference all scale with token counts. The same prompt can tokenize differently from one model to another, so the price for identical content varies.Fairness across languages. This is the part that bothers me most. A tokenizer trained mostly on English handles English very efficiently. Thai, Arabic and many African languages often need far more tokens for the same content. That means higher cost, less room in the context window, and often worse quality because there was less data for them.Reasoning. When one idea gets spread over many tokens, the model has to connect them through attention. Token boundaries that don’t line up with the meaning can also cause odd behaviour. This is part of why models are famously bad at things like counting letters in a word.Practical tips Look at your text in a tokenizer tool, such as OpenAI’s tokenizer playground, to see where the boundaries fall. Expect prompts in different languages to cost different amounts. Structured formats like JSON and markdown tend to tokenize reasonably well, but check rather than assume. Remember that code tokenizes very differently from prose when you estimate size.Where it’s headingPeople are working on character-level fallbacks for rare words, tokenizers learned during pre-training, and models that work directly on bytes and skip tokenization altogether. I’d keep an eye on the byte-level work in particular.Wrapping upTokenizers sit between human language and the model, and they shape cost, context limits and fairness across languages. You don’t need to understand BPE to use an LLM, but knowing it’s there makes a lot of strange behaviour make sense, and it helps you estimate costs more accurately.

title: Mastering Backpressure in Reactive Programming: A Deep Dive
description: Backpressure is the fundamental mechanism that keeps reactive systems from collapsing under load. This deep dive covers what it is, why it matters, and how to implement it correctly across Project Reactor, RxJava, and Akka Streams.
content: Reactive programming is good at handling asynchronous data flows. The trouble starts when a producer emits data faster than a consumer can handle it. Left alone, that mismatch leads to memory blow-ups, a thrashing CPU and failures that spread through the system. Backpressure is how you deal with it.What backpressure isIt’s the consumer’s way of telling the producer “slow down, I can’t keep up.” Instead of quietly dropping messages or falling over, the system applies flow control.Think of a pipe. If you push water in faster than it drains, something gives. Backpressure is the relief valve.What goes wrong without it Unbounded buffers grow until you hit an OutOfMemoryError. The consumer burns CPU working through a huge queue. One slow consumer drags down the whole pipeline. Messages get dropped and nobody notices.That last one is the nastiest, because you find out from a customer.Four strategiesBufferingHold the extra items in a bounded buffer and push back upstream when it fills up.// Project ReactorFlux.range(1, 1000) .onBackpressureBuffer(100) // buffer up to 100 items .subscribe(item -> process(item));Use it when you can’t lose data and the consumer will catch up eventually. Mind the size, because an unbounded buffer isn’t protection at all.DroppingDiscard items when the consumer falls behind. It’s simple, and fine when losing some data doesn’t matter.// RxJavaFlowable.interval(1, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) .onBackpressureDrop() .observeOn(Schedulers.computation()) .subscribe(item -> slowProcess(item));This suits real-time metrics or sensor readings, where an old value is worthless anyway.ThrottlingSlow the producer to a rate the consumer can sustain, instead of buffering or dropping.// Akka StreamsSource.repeat("event") .throttle(10, Duration.ofSeconds(1)) // max 10 elements per second .runWith(Sink.foreach(System.out::println), system);It works when you control the producer and want a steady flow instead of bursts.Requesting (pull-based)The consumer asks for a specific number of items. This is the most precise option and the foundation of the Reactive Streams specification.// Project ReactorFlux.range(1, 1000) .limitRate(10) // pull 10 items at a time .subscribe(item -> process(item));Use it when you want fine control and know roughly how much the consumer can take.The frameworks Framework Default behaviour Useful APIs Project Reactor Error on overflow onBackpressureBuffer(), limitRate() RxJava Depends on the type onBackpressureDrop(), onBackpressureLatest() Akka Streams Propagated automatically throttle(), buffer() All three implement the Reactive Streams specification, which defines backpressure through the Publisher and Subscriber contract. That’s why the ideas carry over from one library to another.Some practical advice Match the strategy to how much the data matters. Financial transactions need buffering. Live metrics can usually be dropped. Always bound your buffers. Test with realistic load. These problems rarely show up at development traffic levels. Measure what your consumer can actually handle before tuning anything. Expose queue depth as a metric, so you see pressure building before it becomes an outage.Wrapping upBackpressure is a normal part of any reactive system under real load. The libraries give you the tools, but choosing between buffer, drop, throttle and request comes down to knowing how much your data matters and how your consumer behaves.

title: Traditional Coding vs AI-Assisted Coding vs Vibe Coding: A New Spectrum
description: Modern software development has evolved into three distinct modes, traditional, AI-assisted, and vibe coding. Understanding when to use each is becoming a core engineering skill.
content: I no longer write code in one way through the day. Depending on the task and what’s at stake, I move between three different modes, and picking the right one has become as important as any technical skill.Traditional codingThis is the old way. I write every line and reason through every decision. It’s slow, but I understand all of it. When something breaks I know where to look, and when a colleague asks why it works a certain way, I can explain.This is where I put anything that has to be right: core domain logic, security-sensitive paths, and problems that are new to me. It’s also how I learn, because writing something by hand teaches you things that reading it doesn’t.AI-assisted codingThis is my default now. I decide the logic and the architecture. The AI handles boilerplate, suggests implementations and takes some of the mental load.It feels like pairing with someone very fast and well-read who occasionally makes things up. I’m still driving, and I still read every line it produces. I just spend less time on the mechanical parts. It suits most day-to-day work: scaffolding, translating a familiar pattern into code, refactoring, and getting a second opinion in code review.Vibe codingThis is the newest mode and the one people misunderstand most. You describe what you want in plain language and iterate on what comes back, rather than working at the level of syntax.The speed is real. For prototypes, exploration and proofs of concept, you can try ten ideas in the time it used to take to build one. I use it for throwaway tools and for getting familiar with an unfamiliar API.But it doesn’t replace engineering knowledge. You need that knowledge to judge what you get back, spot subtle bugs and notice shortcuts that will bite later. Without it you end up with code that arrives fast and is painful to maintain.Choosing between themA single day might go like this. I vibe code to see how a new API behaves, switch to AI-assisted coding to build the real integration, and then write the authentication and error handling by hand.Mixing these up is where trouble starts. Vibe coding a security layer is a bad idea. Hand-writing boilerplate wastes time. And using AI without reviewing the output is just careless.What it means for engineersThere are more ways to build than before, and that’s good. But the fundamentals matter more now, not less. As code gets easier to generate, the valuable part is understanding systems, trade-offs and failure modes well enough to know whether the generated code is any good.The skill I’d work on is noticing which mode you’re in, and whether it’s the right one for the task in front of you.

title: LlamaCoder: Turn Your Idea into an App in Minutes
description: An introduction to LlamaCoder, the AI-powered platform that converts plain language descriptions into functional application code, democratising app development for everyone.
content: LlamaCoder is a tool worth knowing about. You describe the app you want in plain English and it generates working code. It’s built by Together AI on top of large language models.How it worksYou type what you want. The model writes the code, you look at the result, and you ask for changes in plain language until it’s right. The code can be in Python, JavaScript, Swift and others, and the output can target web or mobile.The pitch is that it responds to the goal of what you asked for, not just keywords. Ask for a task manager with due dates and you should get something shaped like one.Where it helps Prototyping. Going from an idea to something you can click takes minutes, which is excellent for testing whether an idea is worth building. Non-developers. Founders, business owners and designers can get a working demo without waiting on anyone. Students. Seeing real code appear from your own idea is a good way to learn. Developers. It’s handy for scaffolding and boilerplate you’d rather not type.It handles the usual suspects well: shop front ends, dashboards, to-do apps, simple social feeds, quizzes and small games.Where I’d be carefulGenerated code is a starting point. You still need to read it, check edge cases, and think about security and maintenance before it goes anywhere near real users. A demo that works on the happy path can hide a lot of problems.The bigger pictureTools like this move the hard part. Writing code gets cheaper, and knowing what to build gets more valuable. Understanding the problem, the users and the trade-offs matters more than typing speed.I don’t think this removes the need for engineers. It shifts our time towards architecture, quality and the awkward problems these tools still don’t solve reliably. For everyone else, it opens up a lot of ability to build things that used to need a developer.You can try it at llamacoder.together.ai.

title: Architectural Trade-off: Serverless APIs vs. Kubernetes APIs
description: A structured comparison of serverless and Kubernetes as API deployment paradigms, trade-offs across operational overhead, scalability, cost, control, and vendor lock-in to help you choose the right architecture for your context.
content: “Should we go serverless or run it on Kubernetes?” comes up on almost every new API project I’m involved in. There’s no single right answer, but there are fairly clear signals pointing each way. Here is how I weigh them up.The basic differenceWith serverless you hand over the infrastructure. You deploy a function or container, set a trigger, and the provider deals with scaling, patching and availability.With Kubernetes you get a platform to build on. You decide how workloads run, how they talk to each other and how they scale. You get control, and you also get the job of running it.Where they differOperations. Serverless wins easily here. No servers to patch and no capacity to plan. Kubernetes needs real expertise: networking, ingress, storage, upgrades and observability. Beyond a certain size that usually means a platform team.Scaling. Serverless scales from zero to a spike without you doing anything. Kubernetes can scale through the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler or KEDA, but you configure it, and you always pay for a baseline of nodes. Scaling to zero needs extra tooling such as Knative. For unpredictable traffic, serverless is the better fit.Cost. Pay-per-use is great for occasional or bursty traffic. At high, steady volume the bill can climb quickly, and a well-packed Kubernetes cluster is often a lot cheaper. Run the numbers for your own traffic, because the break-even point varies.Control. Serverless limits what you can change: runtime versions, execution environment, networking. Kubernetes lets you do almost anything, including custom runtimes, sidecars, service meshes and network policies.Lock-in. Lambda, Cloud Functions and Azure Functions all tie you to a provider, and moving is real work. Kubernetes is more portable. Managed offerings like EKS, GKE and AKS bring a little lock-in at the control plane, but your workloads move fairly easily.Speed to first deploy. Serverless is quicker: upload code, add a trigger, finished. Kubernetes needs image builds, a registry, manifests or Helm charts, and a rollout strategy. A good pipeline hides most of this, but somebody has to build it.Debugging. This is where serverless hurts. Cold starts, short-lived environments and traces spread across many functions are hard to follow. On Kubernetes you can use Prometheus, Grafana, Jaeger and a mesh like Istio, and you control the logging and metrics.State. Serverless expects stateless code, so state goes into DynamoDB, S3, Redis and so on. Kubernetes handles stateful workloads directly with StatefulSets and persistent volumes.A rough guide Situation I’d lean towards Small team, moving fast Serverless Spiky or unpredictable traffic Serverless Little appetite for ops work Serverless High, steady traffic Kubernetes Special infrastructure needs Kubernetes Portability matters Kubernetes Stateful workloads Kubernetes What I’d actually doPlenty of mature teams use both: serverless for event-driven or low-traffic APIs, and Kubernetes for the core services. You don’t have to choose one for the whole company.If you’re unsure, start with whichever your team can run well today. Moving later is a cost, but a team struggling with infrastructure it doesn’t understand costs more.

title: Exploring Threads and Virtual Threads in Java: A Comprehensive Guide
description: A deep dive into traditional Java threads vs virtual threads (Project Loom), how they work internally, when to use each, and why virtual threads are a game changer for I/O-bound applications.
content: Virtual threads arrived as a preview in Java 19 (Project Loom) and became final in Java 21. They’re the biggest change to Java concurrency in a long time, so here is how I think about them next to the threads we’ve always had.Platform threadsA regular Java thread is a thin wrapper over an operating system thread. One Java thread maps to one kernel thread, each with its own stack, and the OS decides when it runs.That’s fine until you have a lot of them. Each thread costs a good chunk of memory, and the OS spends time switching between them. If a thread is blocked waiting for a database or an HTTP call, it still holds all of that. A few thousand threads is about where things start to hurt.Virtual threadsA virtual thread is scheduled by the JVM, not the OS. The JVM runs them on a small pool of carrier threads, which are ordinary platform threads. Their stacks live on the heap and grow only as needed, so they’re cheap. You can have millions.The important part is what happens on a blocking call. When a virtual thread waits on I/O, it unmounts from its carrier, and that carrier immediately picks up another virtual thread. When the I/O completes, the virtual thread is mounted again, maybe on a different carrier, and carries on.   Platform threads Virtual threads Scheduled by OS JVM Cost to create High Very low Practical limit Thousands Millions When blocked Holds an OS thread Frees the carrier Stack memory Large, fixed Small, on the heap Good for CPU-bound work I/O-bound work A web server exampleSay you handle 10,000 concurrent requests and each one spends most of its time waiting on a database.With platform threads you need something like 10,000 OS threads, or a thread pool plus a queue and a lot of tuning. With virtual threads, each request gets its own thread and you write plain blocking code. The carriers stay busy because blocked requests step aside.// One virtual threadThread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { var result = database.query("SELECT ..."); response.send(result);});// Or an executor that creates one per tasktry (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { executor.submit(() -> handleRequest(request));}This is the part I like most. You get the scalability people used to need reactive code for, and your code still reads top to bottom.When I’d use whichStay with platform threads for CPU-heavy work. If the task is crunching numbers and never waits, virtual threads add nothing, because you’re limited by cores anyway. They also make sense when you need tight control over thread behaviour.Reach for virtual threads when the work is mostly waiting: database calls, HTTP calls, file access. Web servers and microservices are the obvious fit.Two things to watch for. Don’t pool virtual threads, since they’re meant to be created freely. And in Java 21, blocking inside a synchronized block pins the virtual thread to its carrier, which can hurt throughput. Newer JDK releases have been improving this, but it’s worth checking on the version you run.SummaryVirtual threads don’t replace platform threads. They cover the large class of server code that mostly waits on I/O, and they let you write it in the simple blocking style while still scaling.

title: Why is Kafka So Fast? Unveiling the Secrets Behind Kafka's Speed
description: A deep dive into the engineering decisions that make Apache Kafka one of the fastest messaging systems, sequential I/O, zero-copy, batching, compression, and intelligent caching.
content: People often ask me how Kafka pushes millions of messages a second on fairly ordinary hardware. There’s no magic in it. It’s a handful of design choices that each cut out a bit of overhead, and they add up.It only ever appendsKafka writes to the end of a log file and never goes back to update anything in the middle. That makes disk access sequential, and sequential reads and writes are far faster than random ones. On spinning disks the difference is huge because the head doesn’t have to jump around. Even on SSDs it still helps.Picture thousands of IoT sensors sending readings. Each reading just lands at the tail of the log. Nothing has to be searched for or moved.Zero-copyThe usual way to send a file over the network is to read it from disk into kernel memory, copy it into your application’s memory, then copy it back into a kernel socket buffer. That’s a lot of copying for no good reason.Kafka uses the sendfile() system call on Linux, which tells the kernel to move the data from the disk cache straight to the network socket. The data never enters the JVM. You save CPU cycles and a lot of memory traffic, which matters a great deal when you’re serving big batches to many consumers.CompressionProducers can compress a whole batch of messages with GZIP, Snappy or LZ4, and consumers decompress it on the other end. The broker generally stores the batch as it arrived.It pays off most with repetitive data such as application logs or JSON events, where you can shrink the payload a lot. Less data on the wire and less on disk.BatchingKafka doesn’t treat messages one at a time. It groups them into batches for both the network and the disk. If you batch 100 metrics together, you do one write and one round trip rather than 100 of each.Every I/O operation has a fixed cost no matter how small the payload is. Batching spreads that cost over many messages. The trade-off is a little extra latency while a batch fills, which you tune with settings like linger.ms and batch.size.The OS page cacheKafka doesn’t build a large cache of its own inside the JVM. It leans on the operating system’s page cache instead. Recently written segments are usually still sitting in memory, so a consumer that is keeping up reads straight from RAM and the disk is barely touched.This also keeps the heap small, so garbage collection pauses stay out of the way. I think it’s one of the smartest choices in the whole design.Putting it together Technique What it saves Sequential I/O Disk seeks Zero-copy Extra memory copies and CPU Compression Bandwidth and storage Batching Per-message I/O overhead Page cache Disk reads None of these is clever on its own. Kafka is fast because it applies all of them together, and because the log-based design makes each one easy to do.
